summary: This standards-track memo defines the Management Information Base (MIB) objects used to monitor and manage TCP implementations through SNMP. It works for both IPv4 and IPv6. It replaces earlier TCP MIB definitions, including RFC 2452 and RFC 2012.

plainLanguage.summary: Network managers like to check how a computer's connections are doing, like a dashboard in a car. This document defines the gauges that show the state of TCP connections.

questions: how to monitor tcp connections with snmp
subtitle: The SNMP objects that let a network manager watch and manage TCP, for both IPv4 and IPv6.

tldr.problem: Earlier TCP MIBs covered only IPv4 in one table, or needed a separate IPv6-specific table, and mixed listening endpoints in with connections.
tldr.mechanism: The TCP-MIB module defines a group of scalars for parameters and statistics, a connection table and a listener table, all indexed with IP-version-neutral address types.
tldr.outcome: It replaces RFC 2012 and RFC 2452, deprecates the old IPv4-only connection table and makes the IPv6-specific MIB historic.

facts.label: Structure
facts.value: Two tables and a group of scalars

today: RFC 4022 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 2012 and RFC 2452, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that replaces or updates it. The text itself says the IPv6-specific MIB of RFC 2452 has moved to Historic status.

sections.title: A MIB for TCP
sections.content:
RFC 4022 defines a portion of the Management Information Base (MIB) for managing implementations of the Transmission Control Protocol. A MIB is a virtual information store of managed objects, generally accessed through the Simple Network Management Protocol (SNMP). The objects are defined with the Structure of Management Information, and this memo gives a module compliant with SMIv2.

The module is called TCP-MIB and works in an IP-version-independent manner. It obsoletes RFC 2452 and RFC 2012. The general management framework is described in RFC 3410.
sections.plainLanguage: A MIB is a list of questions a computer promises to answer about itself. This list is all about TCP.

sections.title: What the Module Contains
sections.content:
The TCP-MIB consists of two tables and a group of scalars.

  • The tcp group of scalars holds parameters of a TCP engine, such as the retransmission algorithm in use and the retransmission timeout values, and statistics such as counters of active and passive opens, input and output segments and errors. Discontinuities in the statistics are identified through the sysUpTime object.
  • The tcpConnectionTable gives status information for all TCP connections handled by the engine, and reports the operating system process that handles each one.
  • The tcpListenerTable gives information about all listening endpoints, again with the handling process.

The module is placed at mib-2 49 and the tcp group at mib-2 6.
sections.plainLanguage: There are three parts: a page of totals and settings, a list of every open conversation, and a list of every program waiting for a new conversation to start.

sections.title: Relationship to Older MIBs
sections.content:
TCP objects were first defined in RFC 1213 and later copied into their own module in RFC 2012 using SMIv2. Earlier versions defined tcpConnTable, which is now deprecated for two reasons. First, it supports only IPv4, and the IETF approach is to write IP-version-neutral MIBs using InetAddressType and InetAddress from RFC 4001 instead of separate definitions per IP version. Second, it mixes listening endpoints with connections, which have different behavior and management access patterns. Splitting it lets each table get its own status and statistics objects.

The IPV6-TCP-MIB from RFC 2452 has been moved to Historic status because separate IP-version-specific tables are no longer used, and implementing RFC 2452 is no longer suggested.

The process identifiers in the new tables are an Unsigned32 that is expected to match hrSWRunIndex of the HOST-RESOURCES-MIB (if smaller than 2147483647) or sysApplElmtRunIndex of the SYSAPPL-MIB. That lets a manager find which connections belong to a given process.
sections.plainLanguage: The old list could only handle one kind of address and kept waiting programs mixed up with running conversations. The new version fixes both by using two tidy lists that work for any address kind.

sections.title: The Scalars and Tables
sections.content:
The scalars include tcpRtoAlgorithm (other, constant, rsre, vanj or rfc2988), tcpRtoMin and tcpRtoMax in milliseconds, and tcpMaxConn, which is -1 when the connection limit is dynamic. Counters include tcpActiveOpens, tcpPassiveOpens, tcpAttemptFails, tcpEstabResets, tcpInSegs, tcpOutSegs, tcpRetransSegs, tcpInErrs and tcpOutRsts. The gauge tcpCurrEstab counts connections in ESTABLISHED or CLOSE-WAIT. Two 64-bit counters, tcpHCInSegs and tcpHCOutSegs, mirror the 32-bit segment counters for fast links.

A row of tcpConnectionTable is indexed by local address type, local address, local port, remote address type, remote address and remote port. Its columns are the connection state and the process ID. A row is transient: it ceases to exist when, or soon after, the connection goes to CLOSED. Implementors must take care that index values do not produce object identifiers with more than 128 subidentifiers, or the data cannot be read with SNMPv1, SNMPv2c or SNMPv3.

A row of tcpListenerTable is indexed by local address type, address and port, and holds the process ID. A listener can be one of three kinds: an application willing to accept both IPv4 and IPv6 uses address type unknown (0) and a zero-length address; one for a single IP version uses 0.0.0.0 or :: with the matching type; and one tied to a specific local address uses that address.
sections.plainLanguage: The first page has simple counters like a car's trip meter. Each open conversation gets a row named by both ends, and each waiting program gets a row named by where it listens.

sections.title: Controlling a Connection
sections.content:
Most objects are read-only, but tcpConnectionState is read-write. Its values are closed(1), listen(2), synSent(3), synReceived(4), established(5), finWait1(6), finWait2(7), closeWait(8), lastAck(9), closing(10), timeWait(11) and deleteTCB(12).

The only value a management station may set is deleteTCB(12), and an agent should answer any other set with a badValue response. Setting it deletes the connection's TCB, as defined in RFC 793, which terminates the connection immediately. As an implementation-specific option a RST segment may be sent to the other end, but RST segments are not sent reliably. The value listen(2) exists only for parallelism with the old table and should not be used, since listeners belong in the listener table.
sections.plainLanguage: A manager can not only look at a conversation but also hang up on it by writing one special value. That is a powerful button, so it needs to be protected.

sections.title: Compliance and Deprecated Parts
sections.content:
The current compliance statement, tcpMIBCompliance2, makes three groups mandatory: the base group of counters and parameters, the connection group and the listener group. The high-capacity group (the 64-bit counters) is mandatory for systems capable of receiving or transmitting more than 1 million TCP segments per second, because that rate makes a 32-bit counter wrap in just over an hour. Write access to tcpConnectionState and support for deleteTCB are not required, and only global IPv4 and IPv6 address types must be supported.

The older tcpConnTable and the IPv4-only compliance statement are kept but marked deprecated. Agents are still encouraged to implement the old objects to interoperate with the deployed base of managers.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a checklist for what a computer must report. Fast computers must also keep bigger counters, so the numbers do not roll over too soon.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The read-write objects tcpConnectionState and tcpConnState allow termination of an arbitrary connection, so unauthorized access could cause a denial of service. Readable objects can be sensitive too. The connection tables reveal active connections and their processes, which an attacker could use to pick attacks and which has privacy implications. The listener objects show which ports are open without the attacker running a port scanner.

SNMP versions before SNMPv3 did not include adequate security, and even on a secure network there is no control over who may read or change the objects. The RFC RECOMMENDS the SNMPv3 security features, including its cryptographic mechanisms, and says deploying earlier versions is NOT RECOMMENDED. Operators must configure access so only legitimate principals can GET or SET the objects.
sections.plainLanguage: The dashboard shows who is talking to whom and which doors are open, and one button can hang up calls. Only trusted people should be allowed near it.

items.label: listen
items.desc: Included for parallelism with the old table; should not be used.

items.label: deleteTCB
items.desc: The only value a manager may set; deletes the TCB and ends the connection.
